title: Overheating at Idle
summary: Common causes, likely diagnostic paths, OBD references, and repair-next steps for overheating at idle.
intro: Overheating at idle usually means coolant flow, heat rejection, or temperature-control strategy is failing when the vehicle is not moving enough air through the cooling system. The best split is whether the engine cools back down once road speed increases or runs hot in every condition.
common_sounds: Temperature climbs while stopped or in traffic
Cooling fan may run constantly or seem out of sync
Heater output may change as temperature rises
Coolant smell or overflow after long idling
quick_checks: Verify coolant level and look for obvious external leaks before replacing parts
Compare scan-data coolant temperature to gauge behavior
Note whether the engine runs cooler once vehicle speed increases
Check for trapped air, poor circulation, or weak heater performance
Inspect whether temperature data looks believable before blaming the sensor or thermostat alone
inspection_priority: Verify coolant level and condition first
Inspect thermostat operation and coolant circulation together
Pressure test the cooling system if coolant loss, smell, or overflow is present
confidence_cues: Further diagnostics may be required if temperature data conflicts with gauge behavior
common_causes: Low coolant level or external coolant loss
Restricted radiator or poor heat rejection
Thermostat sticking or not controlling coolant flow correctly
Cooling fan or fan-control issue in some cases
diagnostic_paths: If the engine overheats mostly at idle and improves on the road, radiator airflow, fan operation, and low-speed heat rejection matter more.
If heater output goes weak and coolant circulation looks poor, water pump and thermostat diagnosis move higher on the list.
If scan data is clearly wrong, verify the coolant temperature signal before making a thermostat-only decision.

diagnostic_path_sections.title: Cooling Flow Path
diagnostic_path_sections.summary: Separate coolant level, thermostat behavior, water pump circulation, and radiator restriction before pricing parts.
checks: Pressure test for leaks before teardown
Compare heater output with coolant temperature
Inspect thermostat and water pump evidence together

diagnostic_path_sections.title: Heat Rejection Path
diagnostic_path_sections.summary: When overheating is strongest at idle, check airflow and radiator heat transfer before assuming engine damage.
checks: Confirm fan operation and airflow through the radiator stack
Check radiator hoses, cap, and coolant condition
Use pressure testing when coolant smell or loss is present
confidence_cues: Pressure test when loss is suspected

recommended_repairs.title: Radiator Replacement Cost
recommended_repairs.description: A practical next path when heat rejection is poor, the radiator is leaking, or flow through the core is restricted.

recommended_repairs.title: Water Pump Replacement Cost
recommended_repairs.description: Relevant when circulation looks weak, heater performance changes, or cooling falls off badly at low speed.

recommended_repairs.title: Thermostat Replacement Cost
recommended_repairs.description: A strong next path when coolant flow control looks erratic or warm-up behavior and overheating overlap.

recommended_repairs.title: Radiator Fan Replacement
recommended_repairs.description: A strong path when overheating improves at road speed and fan command, power, or motor testing points to fan failure.

recommended_repairs.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor Replacement Cost
recommended_repairs.description: Useful when scan data or fan behavior suggests the temperature signal is misleading diagnosis.
